articles.title: Wisconsin farmer Brit Thompson turns a vintage Airstream trailer into an Airbnb, now the rental income outpaces beef and lamb sales: ‘I can make $100 an hour cleaning’
articles.summary: US News: A vintage Airstream trailer parked on a Wisconsin pasture may not sound like a financial lifeline, at least not six years ago. But it is now for Brit .
articles.body: A vintage Airstream trailer parked on a Wisconsin pasture may not sound like a financial lifeline, at least not six years ago. But it is now for Brit Thompson, 33, who runs Pink River Ranch in Wisconsin. She converted her vintage Airstream trailer into an Airbnb, and most of her guests are Chicago-area professionals looking for countryside experiences.Thompson is a farmer, but the unstable economy pushed her to think beyond the box. "I don't want to be out there working my b**t off for $5 an hour when I can make $100 cleaning the Airstream for an hour,” she told MarketScreener. For farmers like Thompson, that difference matters. It can take far longer to earn the same amount by selling beef and lamb through restaurants or farmers' markets.The rise of agritourismBrit Thompson, who also raises animals for meat on her farm, is one of many farmers turning to agricultural tourism, a $4.5 billion industry, according to data from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA). Her trailer now doubles as an Airbnb, offering overnight stays. The decline in income from farming and the rising demand for rural experiences have motivated many farmers in the US to step into tourism.Thompson's ranch sits down the road in Blanchardville, surrounded by Highland cattle, Icelandic sheep, and the kind of landscape that urbanites yearn for. Most of her bookings come from urban areas, including Chicago. Professionals seeking weekend escapes book the stay. Guests visit almost every week during the peak season, drawn by spring-fed trout streams, forested hiking trails, and unpolluted night skies. Needless to say, the income surpasses what her livestock operation generates. This also opens new opportunities for Thompson: she teaches her guests about sustainable grazing, as well as fishing from her riverbank with her five-year-old daughter, who reels in fat catfish with a miniature hot-pink fishing rod.Growing trendThompson is far from alone in recognising the potential of agritourism. Farmers across the US are making the same calculation. They are turning corn mazes, pumpkin patches, farmstays, and cabin rentals into essential revenue streams as traditional agriculture withers. This revenue is nowhere comparable to what most of them make from farming alone. For families trying to hold on to their land, these enterprises mean a lot. They no longer have to sell their land.Farm income has dropped 23% from 2022, according to data from the USDA. This is one of the steepest declines in history, and the American Farm Bureau confirms that the agricultural economy is in recession.Commodity prices for corn and soy hit four-year lows last year. But input costs for seeds, fertiliser, and labour remain punishingly high. Interest rates have climbed. Potential tariffs loom. The maths for row-crop farmers has never been worse."You cannot survive as a family farm only farming," Catherine Topel, 56, a North Carolina hog producer who hosts an Airbnb cabin and campsites through HipCamp, told Reuters."The cabins, the camping – it makes you sustainable and resilient in hard times, and it gives you flexibility to enter into other enterprises instead of toeing the line of what your dad did and what your dad's dad did."Kaylee Heap, 35, co-manager of Heap's Giant Pumpkin Farm in Illinois, where guests pick sunflowers and pumpkins in autumn, ride hayrides, and navigate corn mazes, agrees. "We're able to weather some of these tighter or negative margin years because we've diversified the way we earn money," Kaylee Heap told the news agency. "It's the reason we diversified. If we just focused on row crops, we’d be having a different conversation."Agritourism flourished during the pandemic. People living in cities were in search of socially distanced holiday options, and rural properties offered exactly that. But this wasn't a temporary trend. The number of farmstays listed on short-term rental platforms jumped 77% over five years, roughly double the growth rate of overall listings. Airbnb, HipCamp, Harvest Hosts, and The Dyrt all report substantial increases in farmstay inventory. Not every property is suited for this type of tourism. Countryside properties are at the top of the list, as are secluded locations surrounded by nature.The trend is here to stay, according to Ryan Pesch, an extension educator at the University of Minnesota. “The younger generation finds the farm doesn't have to be this long litany of depression and bad prices. They say: 'Why don't we do this other thing?’ They see opportunities and entrepreneurship," he told Reuters.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: BHOPAL: Madhya Pradesh's Jan Dhan numbers tell two sharply different stories - while the state has 4.76 crore accounts, the average balance in each is just Rs 4,182, among the lowest in the country.More than one-third of these accounts are either inoperative or have zero balance, with 1.36 crore classified as inoperative and another 46.72 lakh carrying no money, according to Union govt data.The information was provided by Union ministry of finance in reply to an RTI query filed by Neemuch-based RTI activist Chandrashekhar Gaur. Its Rs 19,919.10 crore deposit corpus is the sixth-highest among states and UTs, indicating the scale of financial inclusion achieved in terms of account opening.But the low average balance presents a different picture. articles.title: After meeting govt delegation, Manoj Jarange calls off hunger strike on 20th day of agitation, gives govt another three months
articles.summary: CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange on Thursday morning called off his indefinite hunger strike on its 20th day after a go.
articles.body: CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange on Thursday morning called off his indefinite hunger strike on its 20th day after a government delegation held talks with him at Patoda in Beed district and sought three months to address his key demands. This was Jarange’s 11th agitation over the past three years.Cabinet ministers Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil and Dada Bhuse, along with BJP MLA from Ashti Suresh Dhas and BJP MLC Prasad Lad, reached Patoda around 5.40am to discuss Jarange’s demands on behalf of the govt. Following the talks, Jarange announced that he was suspending his fast for 90 days, saying there had been positive discussions on his five main demands.Jarange said the suspension of the hunger strike did not mean the end of his agitation. He gave the government three months to issue the necessary government resolution and implement the Gazetteer-related measures. He also demanded a written assurance that not a single record would be deleted from the nearly 58 lakh records identified in the process of establishing Maratha-Kunbi links.“If the government betrays us, we will go to Mumbai,” Jarange warned, while appealing to over 1 lakh of his supporters who according to him had travelled towards Mumbai, to return home. He said he was prepared to trust the government for three months following the discussions at Patoda.Before announcing the suspension of his fast, Jarange also said Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis was not his enemy and indicated that he would continue to maintain affection for Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde, while making it clear that he would not compromise on the demands of the Maratha community.After ending his fast, Jarange left Patoda for a private hospital in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar city, where he had been undergoing treatment periodically for the past three years.Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news. articles.title: World's richest man Elon Musk has a new home, he is sleeping in a trailer for over 10 days as he wants to be near to ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: ​Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, has a rather unusual new home in Memphis, Tennessee. Instead of staying in a luxury mansion or high-end hotel, Mu.
articles.body: ​Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, has a rather unusual new home in Memphis, Tennessee. Instead of staying in a luxury mansion or high-end hotel, Musk has reportedly been sleeping in an Airstream trailer for more than 10 days while staying close to xAI’s expanding Colossus supercomputer facility. Musk revealed his new “palace” while recording an episode of the All-In podcast with SpaceX president and COO Gwynne Shotwell.The trailer is parked near xAI’s massive infrastructure project, letting Musk stay close to the company’s operations as it races to expand its computing capacity. For someone whose wealth is measured in hundreds of billions of dollars, choosing a compact camper as a temporary home highlights Musk’s long-standing habit of staying unusually close to major projects when he is personally involved.Why Elon Musk is sleeping in an Airstream trailer in MemphisMusk said during the podcast that he was staying in his new “palace” in Memphis. He has not revealed which Airstream model he is using, although some compact models include a sleeping area, kitchen, and bathroom in about 16 feet of space. Gwynne Shotwell described Musk’s decision to stay in Memphis as typical of his approach to major projects.​“This is Elon, by the way, doing what people don’t believe he does. He sleeps on the factory floor. He’s in Memphis, helping build buildings,” she said during the interview. The trailer gives Musk a base close to xAI’s operations as the company continues expanding its physical infrastructure in the city.​Musk is in Memphis as xAI expands Colossus, its giant supercomputer facility built to provide computing power for Grok. The company began construction in 2024 and reportedly completed the initial build in just 122 days.​The scale of Colossus has also created additional computing capacity that xAI has commercialised. The company has struck deals to provide excess capacity to Google and Anthropic.​xAI is continuing to expand its Memphis footprint. In late July, the company announced plans for a fourth data centre, called Minihard, adding to its growing infrastructure network.​Elon Musk has previously slept at his workplaces​The Airstream is not the first time Musk has chosen to stay close to a major business project. According to Walter Isaacson’s biography, Musk and his brother Kimbal slept in their Palo Alto office for six months while building Zip2 in the 1990s. Musk later continued sleeping under his desk while preparing to launch X.com, the online bank that eventually became PayPal. His approach became particularly intense during Tesla’s Model 3 production push in 2017 and 2018.​“It was a frenzy of insanity,” he told Isaacson of that time. “We were getting four or five hours’ sleep, often on the floor. I remember thinking, ‘I’m like on the ragged edge of sanity.’”​Musk also slept at Twitter’s office after buying the company in 2022. He claimed a couch in the company’s seventh-floor library while working on changes to the platform, later saying the company was in a “code-red situation.”​Elon Musk owns luxury homes too​Musk’s preference for basic accommodation during work-intensive periods contrasts with the expensive properties he has owned. He bought a Bel Air mansion for $17 million in 2012, featuring seven bedrooms, 11 bathrooms, a tennis court and a two-storey library. He also owned a $32 million Mediterranean-style estate in Silicon Valley and purchased actor Gene Wilder’s former home in 2013.​In 2020, Musk sold several of his properties and moved to Texas with his then-partner Claire Boucher, known as Grimes. They lived in a small house near SpaceX’s Starbase facility.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Las Vegas company surprises nearly 10,000 workers with more than $70 million in stock; each gets $1,000 for every year they have worked there
articles.summary: US News: Nearly 10,000 employees of Las Vegas-based Station Casinos received an unexpected financial reward as the company marked its 50th anniversary. Accordi.
articles.body: Nearly 10,000 employees of Las Vegas-based Station Casinos received an unexpected financial reward as the company marked its 50th anniversary. According to a September 9 announcement from Red Rock Resorts, the parent company of Station Casinos, eligible full and part-time employees received more than $70 million worth of Red Rock Resorts Class A stock, calculated at $1,000 for every year of service. The announcement was made during a surprise celebration at Red Rock Casino Resort & Spa, where company executives revealed the award to employees. The stock grants recognise workers across the company, with some long-serving employees receiving tens of thousands of dollars in shares.Nearly 10,000 employees receive stockThe stock award covered nearly 10,000 Station Casinos team members, most of whom are based in Southern Nevada. Employees who were working for the company as of September 9, 2026, were eligible for the award. Rather than providing the same amount to every employee, Station Casinos based the value of each grant on the individual's length of service. Under the programme, workers received $1,000 in Red Rock Resorts Class A stock for every year they had worked for the company. Altogether, the grants were valued at more than $70 million.The announcement came during an event at Red Rock Casino Resort & Spa, where Red Rock Resorts Chairman and CEO Frank Fertitta III and Vice Chairman Lorenzo Fertitta revealed the surprise to employees gathered for the company's anniversary celebration.Long-serving employees receive tens of thousands of dollarsBecause the award was tied directly to years of service, some of Station Casinos' longest-serving employees received particularly large stock grants. One of them is Ida Johnson, who began working for the company in 1977. Based on the $1,000-per-year formula, Johnson received $49,000 worth of Red Rock Resorts stock.The company said seven team members who started working in the 1970s at what was then Bingo Palace and remain with the company today each received more than $45,000 in equity. The awards therefore vary considerably depending on an employee's tenure. A worker with 10 years of service, for example, would receive $10,000 worth of stock under the announced formula, while someone with several decades at the company could receive many times that amount.Surprise announcement marks 50 years in Las VegasThe stock distribution formed the centrepiece of Station Casinos' 50th anniversary celebrations. The company's anniversary programme began on July 1 at Palace Station, the property where its story began. The opening celebration included a fireworks and drone show, along with the launch of a new brand identity and the campaign "From Vegas, For Vegas, Always Vegas."Events continued throughout the summer across the Las Vegas Valley. According to Red Rock Resorts, the anniversary programme included live entertainment, commemorative gaming and food-and-beverage offerings, vintage photo booths, employee appreciation events and community volunteer initiatives. The September 9 gathering brought the anniversary programme to a close, while also paying tribute to company founder Frank Fertitta Jr., Station Casinos' history in Las Vegas and employees who have worked for the company over the past five decades.Company says award reflects employee contributionSpeaking at the surprise anniversary ceremony at Red Rock Casino Resort & Spa, Frank Fertitta III, Chairman and CEO of Red Rock Resorts, said the company's founding principles included serving the local community, providing value and taking care of its employees. He described the stock award as a recognition of the people who had helped build Station Casinos over its first 50 years. Lorenzo Fertitta similarly described the award as an investment in the company's nearly 10,000 team members and highlighted their role in building relationships with guests and the Las Vegas community.The surprise element added another dimension to the celebration. Employees arrived at the September 9 event without knowing that the company was preparing to distribute such a large stock award. The announcement meant that the anniversary celebration was not only about marking Station Casinos' history but also about providing employees with Red Rock Resorts stock tied to their years of service.From local casino to five decades of operationsStation Casinos has grown into a major gaming and entertainment operator serving the Las Vegas Valley. Its properties include Red Rock Casino Resort & Spa, Green Valley Ranch Resort Spa Casino, Durango Casino & Resort, Palace Station, Boulder Station, Sunset Station and several Wildfire properties. The company said the 50th anniversary celebration was intended to recognise both its development in Las Vegas and the employees who contributed to that history.With more than $70 million in Red Rock Resorts Class A stock distributed, the anniversary has also become a milestone for thousands of current employees. For workers who have spent decades with Station Casinos, the value of the award is directly tied to the length of time they have remained with the company, making the 50th anniversary celebration a recognition of their years of service as well as the company's history.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Vishwakarma Puja: The Day Nobody Touched the Tools
articles.summary: India News: On Vishwakarma Puja, remembering a leather factory that honoured a Hindu god with Muslim hands participating and biryani from Park Street. Nobody thou.
articles.body: On Vishwakarma Puja, remembering a leather factory that honoured a Hindu god with Muslim hands participating and biryani from Park Street. Nobody thought it needed explaining.Few Hindu festivals can be entered in an office calendar years ahead without consulting a panjika, and Vishwakarma Puja, which falls today, is the most dependable of them, because it is pegged to Kanya Sankranti, the last day of Bhadra, a solar date rather than a lunar one, which is why it generally lands on September 17 every year.It seems only right that the god of engineers should keep better time than most gods.He is, by his résumé, the most accomplished contractor in the Hindu universe. Tradition credits him with Lord Krishna's Dwarka, the golden Lanka that Hanuman ji later set alight, the Pandava capital at Indraprastha and the chariots in which the gods flew. What is less remarked upon is how differently India has chosen to picture him. In the west and north-west he is an old, four-armed man with a white beard and a swan for a mount, which scholars read as a nod to Brahma; in the east he is a young, muscular man with a black moustache, no sons in attendance, and an elephant as his vahana, which suggests God Indra instead. West Bengal, a state with no shortage of bearded elders, decided that its engineer should look like a foreman in his prime, which tells you something about who was doing the worshipping.The flying chariots are how Bengal explains its kites, which dot Kolkata's skies on this day. Hindu mythology is full of gods travelling by air, and Vishwakarma is held to have built the vehicles. The skies over Kolkata on this day used to (and perhaps still do to a lesser extent) fill with petkati and chandiyal, and the morning began with the cry of bhokatta from some rooftop where a boy had just cut a rival's string.Held on the last day of Bhadra, the puja also opens the long Sharodiya season, so the kites were, in effect, the city's first announcement that Maa Durga was on her way. In many Bengali homes the day carries a second observance that has nothing to do with machines. Arandhan, tied to Manasa Puja at Bhadra Sankranti, requires that food be cooked the night before and eaten stale the next day, with cooking itself forbidden; the custom has loosened with modern life but survives in Bengal's villages and in Kolkata's suburbs. The folk phrase for it, Bhadre rendhe, Ashwine khaoa — cook in Bhadra and eat in Ashwin — is as good a summary as any.The puja's real home, though, was never the household. It is observed mostly on factory floors, where workers pray for safe conditions and for their machines to run well, and shrines go up among the tools themselves. Historians studying Kolkata's working class have argued that this was something the workers made their own; Dipesh Chakrabarty wrote about festivals as a source of solidarity inside hostile workplaces, and Leela Fernandes's ethnography of the jute mills treated the building of Vishwakarma pandals as a space of the workers' cultural autonomy.The leather factory: My family's business was a leather factory on Tiljala Road, right behind Don Bosco School, and on this day the more than four hundred men who worked there, nearly all of them Muslim, did not touch their tools. The work that honoured the god had been done the day before, when the craftsmen who spent the rest of the year shaping leather goods turned to sheets of coloured paper instead, cutting out decorations with a skill that matched their day jobs and a gusto that suggested they found paper the more forgiving material. Everything the day required was prepared on the eve, and on the day itself the hands rested.By the time the priest arrived, the god of craftsmen was presiding over a room that craftsmen, most of whom did not pray to him, had dressed for him. I have never been sure how much of the abstention was reverence and how much was the ordinary pleasure of a working day on which no work was expected, and I suspect the men themselves would have found the question tiresome, which is perhaps the point.Then there was lunch. Many factory feasts on the day were vegetarian, a mutton curry being the mark of the more generous units, and ours had apparently decided that gastronomy in this feast was a competitive sport and opted for biryani. The biryani came from Shiraz on Park Street, which opened in 1941 at the Park Street and Mullick Bazar crossing, specialising in Awadhi food, founded by Mohammed Arshad Ali and Ali Hussain, who had come to Calcutta from Bihar. Calcutta's biryani, as every Calcuttan will tell you at length, came down from Awadh with Wajid Ali Shah's exile, and Shiraz's cook Shamsuddin, who joined in the 1970s and reworked its biryani, is said to have had an ancestor who cooked for the nawab.Consider the arrangement then. A feast for the Hindu god of craft, cooked to a deposed Muslim king's recipe by a kitchen that claims descent from his, eaten by four hundred Muslim leatherworkers and one Bengali Hindu family, on a day when the stoves in half of Bengal's kitchens were not supposed to be lit. The factory had solved Arandhan by outsourcing it to a Park Street restaurant, and nobody, as far as I remember, felt the need to hold a seminar about it. (We'd hold a good many seminars or news channel debates now.)The next morning the god went into the waters of the Hooghly, and the men went back to their benches. The tools, having been worshipped for a day, went back to being worked, which is, if you think about it, the only form of worship a tool has ever asked for.Sources/Reading:Dipesh Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (Princeton University Press, 1989)Leela Fernandes, Producing Workers: The Politics of Gender, Class, and Culture in the Calcutta Jute Mills (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1997)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2014, a sheriff’s sale turned up an Apple-1 whose owner had fled the country; the buyer paid without realising exactly what it was, and Christie's sold it for $365,000
articles.summary: US News: Discover the fascinating story of the Ricketts Apple-1 computer, tracing its journey from Steve Jobs' garage to a record-breaking auction at Christie’s for $365,000.
articles.body: In December 2014, a significant Apple-1 computer was sold by Christie’s in New York for $365,000. The auction took place 10 years after Bob Luther attended a sheriff’s sale in Virginia in 2004 and bought an old computer for $7,600. While he was aware that he was acquiring something that was connected to early computers, he had initially not understood the significance of the machine. Christie’s records identify the machine as the “Ricketts Apple-1,” after its original owner, Charles Ricketts. The computer’s history was traced back to its purchase from Jobs in 1976 through later owners and finally to Luther.Ricketts had retained documents connecting the machine to Apple’s earliest days. Among them was a primarily cancelled $600 check dated 27 July 1976, made payable to Apple Computer. Later on, Ricketts annotated the check to record that he had bought the computer from Steve Jobs at his parents’ garage in Los Altos. Eventually, this document helped turn an old circuit board into a valuable artefact.The Apple-1 began when Apple was still a small operationIn 1976, Steve Wozniak designed the Apple-1 and Steve Jobs marketed it. The Computer History Museum records that Wozniak finished the Apple-1 that year and that, alongside Jobs, they secured an order for 50 assembled systems from the Byte Shop in Mountain View, California. Around 200 Apple-1 boards were ultimately sold before the company moved on to the Apple II.The initial machine was very different from the Macintosh and later Apple computers. The Apple-1 was a single-board computer for hobbyists instead of being a complete consumer desktop system; buyers needed additional equipment, including a keyboard and display, to use it as a functioning computer. Though most of these machines were sold via the Byte Shop, Ricketts’ machine had a different story. The auction house described it as the only known surviving Apple-1 with documentation indicating that it was sold directly by Steve Jobs to an individual from his family’s garage.In 1976, Ricketts reportedly acquired the computer for $600. The surviving cancelled check was made payable to Apple Computer instead of Jobs personally. But Ricketts subsequently wrote on it that the machine was purchased from Jobs himself at the family garage. These documents became crucial because Apple-1’s history is usually difficult to construct for many individual machines. In this case, the computer was accompanied by contemporary paperwork that connected it to a named buyer, a specific date and an early Apple location, including a second cancelled check for $193 dated 5 August 1976, which Ricketts annotated as relating to software programmed by Steve Jobs.This machine’s journey from Ricketts to a Virginia sheriffThe auction house’s provenance records that the Apple-1 eventually passed from Ricketts to his son, and then lists Neil Brian Goldberg of Computer Jones and Bruce Waldack, founder of DigitalNation, as owners in 1999. Waldack later experienced financial problems. Reports suggest that he lost his fortune, defaulted on payments for his Learjet and fled to Argentina. Subsequently, his property in Virginia was subjected to a sheriff’s sale, with the Apple-1 being one of the properties that was offered at a self-storage facility in 2004.Through an advertisement, Luther encountered the sale and ultimately purchased the Apple-1 for $7,600 on 14 December 2004. Luther’s purchase did not instantly turn the computer into a valuable collectable. What made things more interesting was the history he subsequently investigated. He spent years tracing the machine’s provenance and interviewing people connected to Apple’s early years. Luther’s research eventually became the basis for his 2013 book, The First Apple. The two cancelled checks, alongside Luther’s book that documented his efforts to investigate the machine and the people connected with its past, helped establish Apple-1’s provenance.Christie’s tested the computer before putting it up for saleThe Apple-1 was not merely an inert historical object. In October 2014, Apple-1 specialist Corey Cohen serviced and successfully started the machine, with reports claiming that Cohen ran the original Apple BASIC program and an original Apple-1 Star Trek game to test it. An original Apple-1 operating manual, a keyboard housed in a wooden case, power equipment and the two 1976 checks were found in the lot.On 3 November 2014, Christie’s announced the auction, describing the machine as the only known surviving Apple-1 documented as having been sold directly by Jobs to an individual. The auction house estimated that it could sell for $400,000 to $600,000. On 11 December 2014, the auction took place in New York, and it was sold for $365,000, below what was originally estimated.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1976, Minnesota residents fought plans for landfills and development along their river valley; 50 years later, the refuge they helped create protects more than 15,000 acres
articles.summary: US News: Half a century ago, a stretch of Minnesota river country faced a very different future. Plans for landfills and development threatened the Minnesota R.
articles.body: Half a century ago, a stretch of Minnesota river country faced a very different future. Plans for landfills and development threatened the Minnesota River bottoms, prompting local residents to push back against a transformation they believed would erase one of the region's most valuable natural landscapes. Today, that fight has left behind an urban wilderness stretching for miles, giving wildlife a protected corridor surprisingly close to the Twin Cities, reports The Minnesota Star Tribune.A half-century of protectionAccording to The Minnesota Star Tribune, the Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge is marking 50 years since the land came under federal protection through the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The refuge now spans more than 15,000 acres along roughly 50 miles of trails and river habitat, stretching from Bloomington to Henderson. Its forests, wetlands, grasslands and river bottoms provide space for birds, insects and other wildlife while giving residents access to nature in a heavily developed part of the state. A 50th anniversary celebration is planned for Sept. 26 at the refuge's visitor center in Bloomington. The event will include a panel featuring current and former refuge managers, along with activities such as archery and a bird walk beginning at 8 a.m., adds the report. Conservation challenges remain part of the conversation and the anniversary panel will examine issues facing the Minnesota River Valley, including water quality, flooding and development along the river's bluffs.Monarchs make their seasonal journeyThe anniversary comes as another natural spectacle unfolds across Minnesota. Monarch butterflies are currently moving through the state on their annual migration toward Mexico. From the North Shore to the Minnesota River Valley, large numbers of monarchs have been spotted, particularly around blazing stars, a late-summer favorite for the butterflies. People hoping to follow the migration can turn to the Project Monarch app and the citizen-science website Journey North, which track sightings and migration activity. Another chance to see the insects is coming Sept. 18, when Gooseberry Falls State Park hosts a Pollinator Party from 10 a.m. to noon. Recent sightings around Two Harbors included thousands of monarchs. The event will also highlight other pollinators and insects, including bumblebees, parasitic wasps and soldier beetles.A new symbol for Minnesota parksThe state's natural landscapes are also getting a chance to appear on the road. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources is accepting designs for a new state parks license plate through Oct. 31. Entrants have been asked to incorporate the North Shore and Lake Superior agate, Minnesota's official state gemstone, into their designs. Once submissions close, a panel will choose three finalists. For a state that has spent decades balancing development with conservation, the license plate contest offers a small reminder of how closely Minnesota's identity remains tied to its parks, waterways and wild spaces.Image Courtesy: istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates.
